title: Check If It Is a Good Array
statement:
You are given an array `nums` of positive integers. Choose any subset of its elements, give each chosen element an integer coefficient (negative coefficients are allowed), and add up the products.

The array is **good** when some choice of subset and coefficients makes this total exactly `1`. Return `true` if `nums` is good and `false` otherwise.
notes:
## Intuition

Every total you can build is a sum of integer multiples of the chosen numbers, so any number that divides all of `nums` also divides every total. If that common divisor is bigger than 1, the total can never be 1. Bézout's lemma gives the converse: integer combinations of a set of numbers can reach exactly their greatest common divisor. So the array is good exactly when the gcd of all its elements is 1. (Leaving elements out never helps, since using a coefficient of 0 is the same as not choosing it.) A slower check tries every divisor `d > 1` of the smallest element and asks whether it divides everything.

## Approach

1. Start `common` at `nums[0]`.
2. For each next number, run Euclid's algorithm on `a = common` and `b = nums[i]`: replace `(a, b)` with `(b, a % b)` until `b` is 0; then `a` is their gcd.
3. Store it back in `common`. Once it reaches 1 it can never grow again, so return `true` right away.
4. After the loop, the array is good only if `common === 1` (this covers a single-element array).

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [12, 5, 7, 23]`, `common = 12`. For `i = 1`: `(12, 5) -> (5, 2) -> (2, 1) -> (1, 0)`, so `common = 1` and the answer is `true` without looking at 7 or 23. Indeed `5·3 + 7·(-2) = 1`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n log M), where M is the largest value: each Euclid run takes O(log M) steps.
- Space: O(1).

## Pitfalls

- Checking pairs is not enough: in `[6, 10, 15]` every pair shares a factor, yet the gcd of all three is 1, so the array is good.
- A single element is good only when it is 1.
- Do not try to search for the coefficients; they can be huge and are not needed.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `common` | gcd of the elements seen so far |
| `a`, `b` | the pair Euclid's algorithm is reducing |
| `remainder` | `a % b`, the next value of `b` |

narration.2: The gcd of just the first element is the element itself.
narration.4: Fold the remaining numbers into the running gcd one at a time.
narration.5: Euclid's algorithm starts from the gcd so far...
narration.7: Keep reducing until the second value becomes zero.
narration.8: The gcd of a and b equals the gcd of b and a % b.
narration.10: The remainder becomes the new second value.
narration.12: When b hits zero, a is the gcd; it becomes the new running gcd.
narration.13: A gcd of 1 can never change again, so the array is already known to be good.
narration.17: After every number, the array is good only if the overall gcd is 1.
